summary: Warfarin and aspirin both increase bleeding risk. Concomitant use significantly raises the risk of gastrointestinal and intracranial hemorrhage. Use with caution; consider gastroprotection.
evidence: Multiple studies show additive antiplatelet/anticoagulant effects. FDA labeling recommends caution. Consider PPI for GI protection.
alternatives: If antiplatelet needed: clopidogrel monotherapy after risk-benefit discussion. For pain: acetaminophen preferred when anticoagulated.

summary: NSAIDs like ibuprofen can increase warfarin effect and bleeding risk. Also GI ulcer risk.
evidence: NSAIDs inhibit platelet function and may displace warfarin from protein binding. Short-term use may be acceptable with monitoring.
alternatives: Acetaminophen for pain/fever. If NSAID required: use lowest dose, shortest duration, consider PPI, monitor INR closely.

summary: ACE inhibitors like lisinopril can cause potassium retention; adding potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics increases hyperkalemia risk.
evidence: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone; risk is dose-dependent and higher in renal impairment. Monitor potassium routinely.
alternatives: Use potassium only when documented deficiency. Consider dietary sources. Avoid potassium-sparing diuretics unless needed.

summary: IV contrast can worsen metformin-associated lactic acidosis risk in renal impairment. Metformin is renally cleared.
evidence: Guidelines recommend holding metformin before and after contrast in at-risk patients; restart when renal function is rechecked.
alternatives: Hold metformin 48h before and after contrast if eGFR <60; recheck creatinine before restarting.

summary: SSRIs like fluoxetine inhibit CYP2D6; tramadol relies on 2D6 for active metabolite. Risk of serotonin syndrome and reduced analgesia.
evidence: Serotonin syndrome cases reported. Tramadol efficacy may be reduced. FDA advises caution with serotonergic drugs.
alternatives: Consider non-opioid analgesia. If opioid needed: morphine or oxycodone (not tramadol). Monitor for serotonin syndrome.

summary: Penicillins can reduce renal clearance of methotrexate, increasing toxicity (myelosuppression, mucositis).
evidence: Mechanism: competition for renal tubular secretion. Case reports and pharmacokinetic data support interaction.
alternatives: Monitor methotrexate levels and CBC if both required. Consider timing or alternative antibiotic when feasible.

summary: Omeprazole (CYP2C19 inhibitor) may reduce activation of clopidogrel and theoretically reduce antiplatelet effect.
evidence: Data conflicting; some studies show reduced efficacy, others do not. Pantoprazole has less 2C19 inhibition.
alternatives: Pantoprazole or H2 blocker (famotidine) preferred if PPI needed with clopidogrel. Or use PPI only when GI risk justifies.

summary: Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4; simvastatin is a 3A4 substrate. Concomitant use increases myopathy and rhabdomyolysis risk.
evidence: FDA limits simvastatin to 20 mg daily when used with amiodarone. Higher doses contraindicated.
alternatives: Use pravastatin, rosuvastatin, or fluvastatin; or limit simvastatin to 20 mg. Monitor CK if symptoms.

summary: Amiodarone increases digoxin levels (reduced clearance and possibly absorption). Risk of digoxin toxicity.
evidence: Well-documented interaction. Reduce digoxin dose by ~50% when adding amiodarone; monitor levels.
alternatives: Reduce digoxin dose and monitor serum levels and clinical signs of toxicity.

summary: Calcium can bind levothyroxine in the gut and reduce absorption. Separate dosing by at least 4 hours.
evidence: Multiple studies show reduced T4 absorption when taken together. Separation restores bioavailability.
alternatives: Take levothyroxine on empty stomach; take calcium at least 4 hours later. Recheck TSH if regimen changes.
